# Domain model

The glossary. When code, docs, issues or UI name a concept, they use the word defined here.

Settled by [Settle the core domain model](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/01-settle-the-core-domain-model.md), against a survey of 10 voice-testing companies, 13 LLM-eval platforms, the model labs, and the classical testing standards. The frame is adapted from Anthropic's [Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents) — egma's spine maps onto theirs, with voice-specific additions where their taxonomy has one agent and voice has two.

## The one-paragraph version

A **test** describes a situation to put an agent in, and names the **personas** who should call about it. Every test has one home inside its **project**: a **test suite**, the named container for tests normally run and reviewed together. Executing one complete suite is a **run**; each test executed once inside it is a **simulation**, which produces a **transcript**, an **outcome**, and **metrics**. **Graders** read those and return verdicts.

## Tenancy

**organization** → **project** → **agent** → **connection**

- **organization** — the customer, and **the only boundary**. Billing, membership, retention, data residency and compliance posture all attach here and nowhere below. Two organizations never see each other's anything.
- **project** — a product area inside it: *Outbound*, *Support*. **A permission scope and a query filter — never a wall.** A project isolates nothing; it labels rows so a permission can name a subset and a query can filter to one. Two projects in the same organization are always queryable together. **Tests, personas and graders all belong to a project**, not to an agent. A test has no agent assignment or applicability list, so the same complete suite can run against any selected agent and the results stay comparable. That comparison is the whole point of testing prompt variants, and it is impossible if each agent owns its own copy. Because the project owns nothing, an asset is never *trapped* in one — the failure that forced Humanloop to rebuild its datasets and graders as new object types. See [What is scoped to a project, and what stays at the organization](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/17-project-versus-organization-scoping.md).
- **membership** — a **user**'s place in an **organization**, carrying their **role**. Access to a project derives from it: **every member of an organization holds their organization role on every project in that organization.** There is no separate project membership, and a person outside the organization has no path to anything inside it.
- **environment** (`staging`, `production`) is **a label on a connection**, never a level in the hierarchy. What actually differs between environments is how you reach the agent.

**The auth provider owns identity; egma owns everything after the front door.** The provider answers only *who is this person and are they logged in*. `organization`, `project`, `membership`, `role`, `invitation` and `api key` are egma's own, and a nullable external-identity column on `user` and `organization` is the provider's entire footprint. See [The auth and tenancy model](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/06-auth-and-tenancy-model.md).

## The agent under test

**agent** — the customer's voice agent. The thing egma is trying to establish trust in. Belongs to a project. It is the stable Egma identity that simulations and production evidence may name; connection records are separate things linked to it, not fields contained inside it.

**agent platform** — the product or framework that runs or exposes an agent, such as Retell, Vapi, LiveKit Agents or Pipecat. An agent platform can offer several connections to the same agent; it is not itself the way egma reaches that agent. A connection can also be platform-agnostic, so its platform may be unknown. Do not call it a runtime: `simulator` is egma's execution system, and earlier records use runtime only for that system. Added 2026-08-09 during the self-hosted phone onboarding grilling; clarified 2026-08-19 during the production-monitoring grilling.

**platform agent reference** — the agent identifier, name, and version that an agent platform reports. Preserve each part when it exists, but require none of them universally: Retell supplies a stable agent identifier and version, while an automatically dispatched or self-hosted LiveKit agent may supply only a name or no platform-agent identity. A name is the value observed for that conversation, not a durable matching key. A platform agent reference is separate from an Egma agent identifier, and name equality never creates an association between them. Added 2026-08-19 during the production-monitoring grilling.

**connection** — how egma's simulator reaches an agent. **Each connection belongs to one agent, and an agent can have many connections.** A LiveKit agent can be reached through its LiveKit room or through a generic phone number; the platform and the connection are separate facts. A connection describes simulation reach. It does not describe how egma receives records of real production conversations.

Every connection is described on separate axes:

- **connection kind** — the direct path egma selects to reach the agent, such as `retell_chat_api`, `phone_number`, or `livekit_room`. The list is open. A future WebSocket or WebRTC endpoint can be a connection kind when it is the path the customer selects. A protocol used only inside another path is an implementation detail, not a second connection kind.
- **access variant** — the configuration and authority egma uses for that connection kind, such as a Retell API key, a public E.164 number, a LiveKit project key pair, or a customer token endpoint. Two access variants can use the same connection kind.
- **modality** — `voice` or `chat`. Decides which layer is under test: chat exercises the harness (prompt, reasoning, tools); voice exercises the harness *plus* the speech stack.
- **product label** — the human name shown for one supported combination of platform, connection kind, access variant, and modality. It explains the choice; it is not another technical identity.
- **environment** — a label.

Current supported combinations are:

| Agent platform | Connection kind | Access variant | Modality | Product label |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Retell | `retell_chat_api` | Retell API key | chat | Retell chat |
| Retell | `phone_number` | Public E.164 number | voice | Retell phone |
| LiveKit Agents | `livekit_room` | Project key pair | voice | LiveKit project credentials |
| LiveKit Agents | `livekit_room` | Customer token endpoint | voice | LiveKit token endpoint |
| Any or unknown | `phone_number` | Public E.164 number | voice | Phone number |

**production ingestion** — how egma receives evidence of real production conversations. It is separate from a simulation connection. An agent platform may have platform-specific ingestion strategies, such as polling Retell's calls API or receiving LiveKit spans through OTLP. Production-ingestion ownership and configuration are settled by their own design, not inferred from a connection kind or access variant. Added 2026-08-19 during the production-monitoring grilling.

**monitoring setup** — the customer configuration that lets egma receive production evidence from one agent platform. Setup starts by selecting the agent platform and then follows that platform's required steps; one setup may select several agents reported by that platform. The platform-specific production-ingestion process runs from this setup. A monitoring setup is not a simulation connection. Added 2026-08-19 during the production-monitoring grilling.

**A simulation records the connection it ran over, and this is load-bearing.** 8 kHz μ-law and WebRTC produce *different units*: the codec destroys information audio graders need and inflates every latency number. Comparing scores across connection types is invalid. See [How to connect to a voice agent, per framework](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/04-voice-agent-connection-per-framework.md).

## The caller

**persona** — the synthetic person who calls the agent. Who they are: manner, patience, accent, background noise, and how they behave under friction. A first-class, reusable, versioned entity. A persona is either **Egma-provided** and shared read-only, or **Custom** and owned by one project.

**persona version** — one immutable, executable form of a persona. It owns the caller's traits and the complete model selection used to bring that caller to life: LLM provider and model, STT provider and model, and TTS provider, model, voice ID, and speed. The technical voice has no second home in traits or platform settings. Editing any of these facts creates a new persona version.

A persona says nothing about *what* the caller wants — that's the test's scenario. The same persona calls about many different things.

Every project carries one active **default persona** — a project choice, not a persona type. A new project points at Egma's shared default persona. A project may point at any active Egma-provided or Custom persona available to it instead. A default cannot be archived until the project pointer moves. A test created naming no callers receives this pointer, so authoring a first test never waits on authoring a caller.

In a transcript the two speakers are labelled **`human:`** and **`agent:`**.

> Renamed from `digital human` on 2026-08-05 (public issue #8). `digital human` was originally chosen over `persona` for saying plainly that the caller is synthetic — accepting that users arriving from other tools would say "persona" and need correcting. They did say it, and the correcting bought nothing: `persona` is the voice industry's near-unanimous term, and now it is egma's. Also considered and still not chosen: `simulant`, `virtual human`, `synthetic user`, `phantom`, `surrogate`.

## The specification

**test** — one authored specification. Anthropic's *task*. Owned by the project and contained by exactly one test suite. It never belongs or applies to named agents. It holds:

- **the scenario** — the situation, as the test's own content. What the caller wants and the circumstances. Not a separate entity.
- **personas** — an array. One to start; several when a scenario should be checked against several kinds of caller. Three personas on a test means running it produces three simulations.
- **expected behaviors** — an ordered list of **plain sentences** about what should happen, **at least one, enforced at write time**. A test with no expected behaviors is unfalsifiable and is rejected, not silently accepted. The sentences carry no metadata: per-behavior priorities were retired 2026-08-14 (grader-redesign grilling) — under binary scoring every behavior must hold, so a priority had nothing left to say. Replaced *the expected outcome* (one paragraph of end state) on 2026-08-05 in the test-factory grilling: a list buys per-behavior verdicts, and Coval deprecated its output-shaped field for exactly this shape. Entries may describe conduct along the way or the state afterwards; true outcome *verification* against customer systems returns with verification hooks.
- **graders** — none named on the test. The project's seeded expected-behaviors copy and every other running grader apply to every test on their own; per-test attachment (the grader array and `test_grader` junction) was dropped 2026-08-14 and returns, if needed, as grader-side filters in the custom-grader era. Every test can still fail from birth — the seeded copy sees to it. History: ADR-0004 superseded *at least one grader at write time*; [ADR-0009](docs/adr/0009-grader-library-and-running-copies.md) superseded the array.

**Tests are modality-agnostic.** A test never mentions voice or chat. This buys the best diagnostic in the product: run the same test over chat and over voice, and the difference isolates the failure. Passes on text, fails on voice → the prompt is fine and the speech stack is broken. Fails on both → it's the reasoning.

**test suite** — an unversioned, named container for tests normally run and reviewed together. A user creates it before the first test; the one clean-cutover exception is the ordinary `Default` suite created around existing tests by the one-time migration. Suites are flat, unordered, and may be empty. Every test belongs to exactly one suite for its lifetime; tests never move between suites. A suite's name may change. Deleting a suite deletes every test it contains, after a warning, and neither the suite nor those tests can be restored; post-cutover runs that already used them remain historical facts and show the suite's last name marked as deleted. One test may also be deleted permanently without deleting its suite. A suite never carries graders, agents, connections, or execution settings. See [ADR-0013](docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md).

## Mock tools

**mock tool** — a project-owned stand-in for one of the agent's tools: the tool's name, and the answer egma serves when the agent calls it during a simulation. The answer may be an error — that is how a test forces the failure branch — and may carry a delay, so a mocked backend takes as long as the real one would. **Matching is by tool name, strictly: one answer per tool.** A mock tool never reads a call's arguments; wrong arguments are caught by grading, not matching, because the arguments are on the record either way. Chosen over `tool mock` because it is the word users arrive with (Cekura, Vapi) — the persona lesson, applied the cheap way this time. Added 2026-08-09, mock-tools grilling.

**Project mock tools apply to every test by default; a test overrides per scenario, and the override is the branching mechanism.** "The calendar has no free slots" is the same test with one mock tool overridden. A mock tool may name the agents it applies to (default: all) — agent *affinity* without agent *ownership*, so prompt variants are always tested against one world and their comparison stays honest. Mock tools are deliberately **unversioned** — the one authored thing that is (decided 2026-08-09, same grilling): an edit overwrites, and history lives elsewhere — every answer a simulation was served is on that simulation's record, and a run snapshots its resolved answers at creation, so one run always sees one world. The never-overwritten rule stands everywhere else; versioning returns if cross-run change detection ever demands it.

**Unmocked tools run real, and unobserved.** A tool no mock tool covers runs its real implementation natively — egma is not in that path and does not see the call. Decided 2026-08-09, reversing the same session's earlier design (every call observed and stamped `pass-through`): the receipt required wrapping every tool, and wrapping only what egma answers won. The record's honesty is at the **tool grain**, from discovery: which of the agent's tools were covered by mock tools and which were not. That is the **coverage stamp** (`mock_tool_coverage` on a simulation), and its absence is a fact of its own — no stamp means nothing ever asked the agent what tools it has, while three empty lists mean the asking happened and nothing came back. A mocked simulation and an unmocked one remain **different units**, exactly as two audio bands are, and the record is what enforces it.

**egma SDK** — the piece of egma a customer installs inside their own agent's process. Its first job is the mock-tools seam for LiveKit agents: report the agent's tool list when the session starts, then wrap exactly the tools this simulation mocks — each wrapped call goes to egma's participant over in-room RPC and egma answers with the mock. Tools egma does not answer stay native. In a room with no egma participant it is inert, so production behavior is untouched by construction. One public verb, awaited once where the session is built: `await mockable(agent, ctx, session)` — the wait is structural, because the tool list has to have been reported before the agent's first tool call. See [ADR-0008](docs/adr/0008-mock-tools-are-served-over-in-room-rpc.md). Added 2026-08-09, mock-tools grilling.

## Execution

**run** — one execution of one complete test suite against one agent over one connection. Every test in the suite runs; no agent relationship filters the suite. ISTQB's *test run*: *"the execution of a test suite on a specific version of the test object."* The object a results page shows and CI gates on. The UI labels the surface **Simulations → Runs** in navigation — the group supplies the first word — and **simulation runs** in page headings; the word everywhere else stays `run` (settled 2026-08-16, monitoring grilling; regrouped 2026-08-19, product-UI ticket 17). A run may have a user-written name, but does not require one. …1280 tokens truncated…ans, the pages' analytics and errors, the box's vitals. Never a customer's data and never in ClickHouse — `trace` and `span` stay conversation words, and egma's own telemetry never shares the trace store's pipe. Behind one flag, `EGMA_TELEMETRY`, off by default everywhere; hosted egma turns it on and points it at PostHog and CloudWatch. Added 2026-08-17, observability effort; see [ADR-0010](docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md).

## Judging

**grader** — a running copy of a grader-library entry: the row that judges, and the thing verdict rows name. Created by pressing **Use** on a library entry, or seeded at project creation. It points at its entry (`library_id` — the connecting tissue, never null, never orphaned: deleting a referenced entry is refused), carries the entry's `type`, and holds its **filled-in values** — latency's `[{metric, bound}]` — in immutable versions; editing the values mints the next version, and a run pins the versions it executed. Each grader version also points at one immutable grader-library definition version. The prompt or code is shared once at the library layer, never copied into each project, while the exact definition used by an old run stays reconstructable. Redefined 2026-08-19, model-execution cutover; the word previously named the authored logic itself.

**The distinction that matters: a metric measures, a grader judges.** Nobody wrote down that the call took four minutes — it just happened. Someone had to decide that verifying identity before disclosing a balance matters, and write the criteria. That's the line.

They connect in one direction: **a grader may read a metric.** *"Fail if p90 response time exceeds 2 seconds"* is a grader whose input is a measurement. So latency is always known, and only becomes a verdict if you ask for one.

A grader declares:

- **required** — `true` (default): the test cannot pass unless this copy fully passes. `false`: a **diagnostic** — judged, displayed with its fraction, never able to fail anything. τ2-bench's outside-the-reward-basis components, and the only loudness switch v0 has. Replaces the P0/P1/P2 priority ladder, retired 2026-08-14, grader-redesign grilling.
- **its scope** — the whole answer to where the copy applies: two switches — **judges simulations** (default on) and **judges production** (default off, with the production sampling rate) — and a **filter** under each switch. `both` retired 2026-08-20, grader-scope grilling: it was two switches written as one word, and the one word hid the two opposite safe defaults (simulations exist to be judged; production judging spends money on traffic nobody asked egma to create). Dormant is **no copy at all** — the switches say where an existing copy applies, not whether it exists; pressing Use is still the enabling and deleting the copy is the off-switch.
- **which modalities it can score** (declared by its library entry). *"Didn't interrupt the caller"* is meaningless on chat. A grader that can't score the modality is **skipped**, and the results view must say *skipped*, not *failed*.

**grader library** — the shelf of grader definitions: `grader_library` holds each stable library identity and immutable definition versions hold its executable prompt, output definition, parameter schema, or code. An entry declares its **type** — `llm_as_judge` or `code`; reserved: `human`, `ml_model`, `external`. **Owner derives from tenancy**: null organization and project means egma owns the entry — the one deliberate exception to hard-required tenancy — seeded from a catalog in egma's code. When an Egma release changes a definition, reconciliation mints one new shared definition version and new grader versions for active running copies. New runs pin those versions; old runs keep the old definition through their already-pinned grader versions. No definition is copied per project, and no catalog edit changes the meaning of an old verdict. Team-authored entries land in the same library with tenancy set, when custom authoring arrives. Redefined 2026-08-19, model-execution cutover.

**predefined grader** — a library entry egma owns and ships. v0 ships two: **expected_behaviors** (`llm_as_judge`) and **latency** (`code`). Replaces *built-in grader*, 2026-08-14 — `predefined` is the word users arrive with (Cekura), the persona lesson applied the cheap way again.

**rubric** — the criteria text an `llm_as_judge` grader carries. Anthropic's word. Added 2026-08-07; repointed from the retired `llm_rubric` type, 2026-08-14.

**assertion** — one 0-or-1 check inside a grader. A grader holds one or more assertions, and each is judged in isolation: for an LLM-judged grader, one independent judge call per assertion — Anthropic's per-dimension isolation, which is how the engine has run since the grading effort. The expected-behaviors grader's assertions are the test's own expected behaviors; a code grader's assertions are the entries in its configuration. Un-banned and adopted 2026-08-14, grader-redesign grilling: the word once banned as a synonym for a whole grader now names the level below it, and the old ban stands exactly there — an assertion is never a grader. One word at every layer: the verdict store's column is `assertion` too (renamed from `dimension` by the same grilling — the store is pre-launch and small, so the rename is cheap).

**Applicability: a running copy applies to everything its switches and filters allow.** There is still no per-test attachment — the `test_grader` junction stays dropped, and a test names no graders; narrowing is declared grader-side, so a check written once judges everything it covers without anyone remembering to attach it. A copy whose switch or filter excludes a conversation writes no verdict rows at all — absent, never `skipped`, which keeps meaning "applied but could not score the modality". Settled 2026-08-20, grader-scope grilling: the filters deferred by the grader-redesign spec arrived, per side — see the grader-scope spec. **Never attached to a suite** stands untouched.

**filter** — the where/and rows under one switch of a running copy's scope: `{fact, any_of | none_of, values}`, rows joined by AND, at most one row per fact, values inside a row OR'd; empty means everything that switch allows. Facts come from a **fact catalog** in egma's code that declares each fact's value source, its operators, and which sides can answer it — `agent` on both sides, `test` on simulations only in v1 — so the production builder never offers a fact a live call cannot answer, and an unanswerable rule is unrepresentable rather than refused. A filter is live and unversioned, like the switches: what a grader judges by is versioned; where it applies is not. Added 2026-08-20, grader-scope grilling.

**scope_editable** — on the library entry: whether copies of it may re-aim their scope. Using an egma-defined grader means using it **as is** — you edit what egma allows; false locks the whole scope (switches, rate, both filters) on every copy, seeded or Use-created. expected_behaviors ships locked (judges simulations on, production off, no filter), which also enforces that it can never judge a live call — a production trace has no test to judge against; latency ships editable. `required` is not scope — how loudly, not where — and stays editable on locked copies. Forking a grader is not a v1 concept. Added 2026-08-20, grader-scope grilling.

**expected-behaviors grader** — the predefined `llm_as_judge` entry that judges a simulation against its test's expected behaviors. Its assertions are the test's own sentences — supplied per test at judging time, one isolated judge call each ([ADR-0007](docs/adr/0007-grading-runs-in-its-own-service.md)) — so the entry itself defines no assertions and **Use** asks nothing. In the library like any entry, and **auto-seeded as an active running copy in every new project** (judges simulations only, required, locked as-is by its entry's `scope_editable: false`), so a first run is judged with zero setup. Structurally simulations-only: a production trace has no test, and the locked scope is what enforces it. Supersedes ADR-0004's never-a-row clause — see [ADR-0009](docs/adr/0009-grader-library-and-running-copies.md); falsifiability still lives on the behaviors list, required non-empty at write time, exactly as ADR-0004 placed it.

**verdict** — `passed`, `failed`, `skipped`, or `errored`, written **one row per assertion**. `skipped` and `errored` are load-bearing and must never be collapsed into `failed`: a test that couldn't run is not a test that failed, and a check that couldn't read its inputs didn't fail either. A verdict row carries a 0–1 score, a one-line rationale (on an `errored` row, the plain-prose reason judging broke), the turns it cites, and its assertion's **key** — the behavior's position in the pinned test version, the config entry's index — never the content, which is read from the pinned versions at display time. **Scoring is binary**: a grader's fraction (passed ÷ counted, skipped out of the denominator) is reported for diagnosis and decides nothing; a test passes in a run when every applicable `required` copy fully passes across all its simulations. Overall outcomes are always computed from verdict rows at read time, never stored. Thresholds, weights, and human corrections are designed and deferred — see the grader-redesign spec. Extended 2026-08-07; rewritten 2026-08-14, grader-redesign grilling.

## The onboarding surface

**wizard** — the complete terminal experience `npx egma` presents when run bare: its UI, the intelligent work performed by the developer's local coding agent, and the deterministic work performed through the same CLI modules as the headless verbs. It takes a developer from nothing to a running first run. The internal split is not a second customer experience, and the wizard is never a second code path. Clarified 2026-08-09 during the self-hosted phone onboarding grilling; originally added 2026-08-06 ([ADR-0006](docs/adr/0006-onboarding-wizard-drives-the-customers-coding-agent.md)).

**egma folder** — the `egma/` directory in the customer's repo: project, agent, and connection config; one directory per test suite under `tests/`; a `suite.yaml` carrying that suite's stable ID and mutable name; one markdown file per test inside its suite directory; and one file for the project's mock tools. One repository may contain several suites. A suite directory is only a local path: moving or renaming it changes no product identity or name. Editing `suite.yaml` changes the suite name on push. The folder is committed, never gitignored; nothing secret ever lands in it. The platform remains the store of record — the folder is a working copy.

**platform binding** — the non-secret platform URL written in `egma/config.yaml` beside the resource identifiers that platform owns. It chooses the platform that receives those identifiers; credentials and a platform-instance identity are never part of the binding. An unbound repository uses hosted egma at `app.egma.ai`. See [ADR-0012](docs/adr/0012-agent-repositories-bind-to-a-platform-url.md).

**pull / push** — the explicit sync verbs between the egma folder and the platform, on git's model: `pull` writes the platform's current versions into files; `push` uploads and **refuses** when the platform has moved since the last pull. **That refusal is a property of versioned things**: a test earns it, and so do the mock-tool overrides that version with it. A project mock tool is unversioned by decision, so it has no version to have moved — pushing `egma/mock-tools.md` is last-write-wins, and a teammate's edit in between is not detected; the run's snapshot and the answers on the record carry that history instead. Sync is always a verb a developer runs, never a background process — two silently-syncing authoring surfaces are the documented failure (Humanloop's copy-drift).

## Banned words

Do not use these — in code, schema, API, docs or UI.

| Don't use | Why | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `eval`, `evaluation` | Everyone says it, nobody agrees what it points at | nothing — informal prose only |
| `evaluator` | Half the industry means the test, the other half the thing scoring it | `grader` |
| `scorer`, `check` | Borrowed words for the judging job — one word per level | `grader` for the authored logic, `assertion` for one criterion inside it |
| `dimension` | The verdict store's old column name for it — one entity, one word, at every layer including storage | `assertion` |
| `gate` | Considered for the must-pass flag during the grader redesign, not chosen | `required` |
| `built-in grader` | Renamed 2026-08-14 — `predefined` is the word users arrive with (Cekura) | `predefined grader` |
| `metric` *for scoring logic* | A metric measures, a grader judges | `grader` |
| `digital human` | The old name, renamed 2026-08-05 — one entity, one word | `persona` |
| `simulant`, `virtual human`, `synthetic user`, `digital twin` | Considered, not chosen | `persona` |
| `scenario` *as an entity* | It's what a test says, not a thing of its own | a field on `test` |
| `session` *for a conversation* | Same thing as a simulation | `simulation` |
| `trial`, `attempt`, `iteration` | Running a test twice just makes two simulations | `simulation` |
| `call` | Half of them are chats | `simulation` |
| `conversation` | Same thing as a simulation | `simulation` |
| `caller` | Breaks the moment it's a chat | `persona` |
| `result` *as an entity* | A result is "passed" or "failed" — it isn't the recording | `verdict`, or the simulation itself |
| `experiment`, `batch` | Borrowed from a different world | `run` |
| `expected outcome` *as a test field* | Replaced 2026-08-05 — the test's expectations are a list of behaviors, not one paragraph of end state | `expected behaviors` |
| `tool mock` | The inverted form of the entity's name — one entity, one word | `mock tool` |
| `stub`, `fake` *for a mock tool* | Same job, one word | `mock tool` |

**One carve-out, and it is not a loophole.** `session` **is the right word for a signed-in browser session**, and the ban does not reach it. The auth provider owns a `session` table, the provider seam's fourth method is `revokeSession`, and [ADR-0001](docs/adr/0001-auth-provider-owns-identity-only.md) and the control-plane spec both require the word in that sense — so the unqualified ban forbade what the decision records mandate, which is how a glossary stops being consulted. Added 2026-08-01 after the control-plane code review found the contradiction, with roughly ninety correct uses already in the codebase. The ban stands exactly where it was aimed: **`session` never names a conversation.** A simulation is a simulation.

The same carve-out covers one more seam, for the same reason: **the Agent Client Protocol names its connection to a driven coding agent a `session`** (`session/new`, `session/prompt`, `session/request_permission` are the wire methods), and [ADR-0006](docs/adr/0006-onboarding-wizard-drives-the-customers-coding-agent.md) mandates that SDK — so the CLI's ACP seam uses the protocol's word as-is, exactly as the auth seam uses the provider's. Added 2026-08-06 after the walking-skeleton code review hit the contradiction. Both carve-outs point the same direction: a `session` is standing machinery you connect to, never the conversation a persona has with an agent.

## Reserved words

Good words. Each means exactly one thing and is never borrowed for another.

| Word | Always means | Never means |
|---|---|---|
| `user` | the developer using egma | the persona |
| `customer` | the organization paying for egma | the persona |
| `agent` | the voice agent under test | egma's side of the call |
| `human` | the caller's side of a transcript | a real person reviewing results |
| `project` | the tenancy container below the organization | any resource inside one — LangSmith's collision, where "project" is a resource four levels beneath a "workspace" container |
| `trace` | one conversation end to end, simulated or real — a storage-layer word that never appears in a UI | a UI-facing name for a simulation |
| `span` | one timed thing inside a trace — a storage-layer word that never appears in a UI | a turn specifically; a turn is one kind of span |

`trace` and `span` were put on this list by [The unified ClickHouse trace schema](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/09-unified-clickhouse-trace-schema.md), which needed a word for a conversation that might not be a simulation: a production trace has no test, no run and no persona, so `simulation` cannot name it. A simulation *is* a trace — one carrying a `run_id`. Recorded here 2026-08-02 after a trace-store code review found the ticket's instruction had never landed in this file.

`global` was briefly the label over the standing pair (Agents, Graders), added 2026-08-19 by [17 — Group the navigation](.scratch/product-ui/issues/17-group-navigation-under-global-simulations-and-monitoring.md) with its objection recorded: nothing under it was global, and a reader could predict organization-wide settings behind the word. The recorded reopen condition — first-user evidence of the misread — arrived 2026-08-20 as the developer's own first look, and the label was dropped the same day: the pair now sits as an unlabeled cluster above Simulations and Monitoring. The word is free again and means nothing in this product.

## Mapping to Anthropic's taxonomy

| Anthropic | egma | Note |
|---|---|---|
| evaluation suite | **test suite** | egma's is a named container, not a saved selector or execution plan |
| task | **test** | |
| trial | **simulation** | |
| *(unnamed)* | **run** | Anthropic leaves this slot empty; 8 of 10 voice vendors call it a run |
| transcript / trajectory | **transcript** | |
| outcome | **outcome** | |
| grader | **grader** | |
| assertion (sometimes called checks) | **assertion** | Same word; one 0-or-1 check inside a grader |
| tracked metrics | **metric** | A field, not an entity |
| agent harness | **agent** + **connection** | Split, because reaching the agent is a first-class problem in voice |
| *(none)* | **persona** | Anthropic's taxonomy has one agent; a voice conversation has two participants |

## Deferred

Named here so the boundary is clear; decided elsewhere.

- **What a grader is made of** was settled 2026-08-07 by the grading effort (`.scratch/grading/spec.md`) and **re-settled 2026-08-14 by the grader redesign** (`.scratch/grader-redesign/spec.md`): a library of definitions, running copies, assertions, binary scoring. Where the two disagree, the redesign wins.
- **Thresholds, weights, filters, custom authoring, human corrections, the `ml_model` and `external` types, and any warn tier** — each designed with a named home and deferred, in the grader-redesign spec's future-work section. Deliberately not sketched anywhere else, so the sketch cannot fork.
- **Classification** — labels that segment without judging: sentiment, topic of a conversation, where it dropped off. A third concept beside measure (a number, automatic) and grader (a verdict, chosen): a label, chosen. Every surveyed vendor ships it; none names it. Deliberately deferred so labels are never wedged into verdicts.
- **Whether a persona behaves like a real caller**, and how egma would claim it does, is not yet specified. It is the credibility floor of the product.
- **Where personas come from.** Research strongly favours grounding them in the customer's own recordings over describing them from demographics.
- **Chain-consistent mock worlds** — bundles that keep `lookup_user` → account → booking data coherent across mock tools (the "John Smith world"). Deliberately deferred: project defaults plus per-test overrides carry v1, and a bundle entity can grow out of them if incoherence actually bites. Named 2026-08-09, mock-tools grilling.

# egma — internal agent instructions

This private repository is the planning half of the public Egma code repository. Read this file whenever it is present.

## Repository roots

- **Planning root:** the Git repository containing this file. From the Egma code root, its path is `egma-planning/`.
- **Code root:** the parent Egma Git repository when this checkout is nested in its standard internal location.

All internal plans, tickets, research, domain terms, architecture decisions, and specifications live in the Planning root. Source code, tests, builds, and public documentation live in the Code root.

These are separate Git repositories. Commit planning changes in the Planning root and code changes in the Code root. A request to commit changes can require one commit in each repository.

## Agent skills

### Planning root

Repository configuration overrides the default planning paths in installed Matt skills.

Resolve these paths from the Planning root:

- `CONTEXT.md`
- `docs/adr/`
- `docs/agents/`
- `.scratch/`
- `.out-of-scope/`

Resolve every other repository path from the Code root unless the task says otherwise. Skill-local paths, such as a template beside a `SKILL.md`, remain relative to that skill.

### Issue tracker

Use the local Markdown tracker under `.scratch/<effort>/`. See `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`.

The Planning root is private and separately version-controlled. All internal documentation stays here. This positional rule removes the need to decide which parts of a planning document are safe to publish.

### Triage labels

Use the five canonical triage roles and write their values to the issue file's `Status:` line. See `docs/agents/triage-labels.md`.

### Domain docs

This project uses one domain context. Use `CONTEXT.md` as the glossary and `docs/adr/` for architecture decisions. See `docs/agents/domain.md`.

The settled vocabulary is `test` → `test suite` → `run` → `simulation`, with `grader` for judgment logic, `persona` for the synthetic caller, and `agent` only for the customer's agent under test. `eval` names nothing.

## Matt skill maintenance

When the developer invokes `/update-matt-skills`, read and follow `.agents/skills/update-matt-skills/SKILL.md`. The skill updates the public copies, restores their generic path-routing block, and verifies every tracked Matt skill.

## Pull-request reviews

Greptile reviews every public pull request automatically and can comment in several waves. Keep fixes in the same branch. Answer a review thread when its recommendation is not applied. A pull request is ready to hand off when every Greptile thread is fixed or answered.

## Keep the public repository quiet

The public `AGENTS.md` carries one conditional pointer to this file. Other public files must stand on their own and must not explain the private planning repository. Write public documentation for external readers instead of copying internal material.

# Domain model

The glossary. When code, docs, issues or UI name a concept, they use the word defined here.

Settled by [Settle the core domain model](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/01-settle-the-core-domain-model.md), against a survey of 10 voice-testing companies, 13 LLM-eval platforms, the model labs, and the classical testing standards. The frame is adapted from Anthropic's [Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents) — egma's spine maps onto theirs, with voice-specific additions where their taxonomy has one agent and voice has two.

## The one-paragraph version

A **test** describes a situation to put an agent in, and names the **personas** who should call about it. Every test has one home inside its **project**: a **test suite**, the named container for tests normally run and reviewed together. Executing one complete suite is a **run**; each test executed once inside it is a **simulation**, which produces a **transcript**, an **outcome**, and **metrics**. **Graders** read those and return verdicts.

## Tenancy

**organization** → **project** → **agent** → **connection**

- **organization** — the customer, and **the only boundary**. Billing, membership, retention, data residency and compliance posture all attach here and nowhere below. Two organizations never see each other's anything.
- **project** — a product area inside it: *Outbound*, *Support*. **A permission scope and a query filter — never a wall.** A project isolates nothing; it labels rows so a permission can name a subset and a query can filter to one. Two projects in the same organization are always queryable together. **Tests, personas and graders all belong to a project**, not to an agent. A test has no agent assignment or applicability list, so the same complete suite can run against any selected agent and the results stay comparable. That comparison is the whole point of testing prompt variants, and it is impossible if each agent owns its own copy. Because the project owns nothing, an asset is never *trapped* in one — the failure that forced Humanloop to rebuild its datasets and graders as new object types. See [What is scoped to a project, and what stays at the organization](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/17-project-versus-organization-scoping.md).
- **membership** — a **user**'s place in an **organization**, carrying their **role**. Access to a project derives from it: **every member of an organization holds their organization role on every project in that organization.** There is no separate project membership, and a person outside the organization has no path to anything inside it.
- **environment** (`staging`, `production`) is **a label on a connection**, never a level in the hierarchy. What actually differs between environments is how you reach the agent.

**The auth provider owns identity; egma owns everything after the front door.** The provider answers only *who is this person and are they logged in*. `organization`, `project`, `membership`, `role`, `invitation` and `api key` are egma's own, and a nullable external-identity column on `user` and `organization` is the provider's entire footprint. See [The auth and tenancy model](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/06-auth-and-tenancy-model.md).

## The agent under test

**agent** — the customer's voice agent. The thing egma is trying to establish trust in. Belongs to a project. It is the stable Egma identity that simulations and production evidence may name; connection records are separate things linked to it, not fields contained inside it.

**agent platform** — the product or framework that runs or exposes an agent, such as Retell, Vapi, LiveKit Agents or Pipecat. An agent platform can offer several connections to the same agent; it is not itself the way egma reaches that agent. A connection can also be platform-agnostic, so its platform may be unknown. Do not call it a runtime: `simulator` is egma's execution system, and earlier records use runtime only for that system. Added 2026-08-09 during the self-hosted phone onboarding grilling; clarified 2026-08-19 during the production-monitoring grilling.

**platform agent reference** — the agent identifier, name, and version that an agent platform reports. Preserve each part when it exists, but require none of them universally: Retell supplies a stable agent identifier and version, while an automatically dispatched or self-hosted LiveKit agent may supply only a name or no platform-agent identity. A name is the value observed for that conversation, not a durable matching key. A platform agent reference is separate from an Egma agent identifier, and name equality never creates an association between them. Added 2026-08-19 during the production-monitoring grilling.

**connection** — how egma's simulator reaches an agent. **Each connection belongs to one agent, and an agent can have many connections.** A LiveKit agent can be reached through its LiveKit room or through a generic phone number; the platform and the connection are separate facts. A connection describes simulation reach. It does not describe how egma receives records of real production conversations.

Every connection is described on separate axes:

- **connection kind** — the direct path egma selects to reach the agent, such as `retell_chat_api`, `phone_number`, or `livekit_room`. The list is open. A future WebSocket or WebRTC endpoint can be a connection kind when it is the path the customer selects. A protocol used only inside another path is an implementation detail, not a second connection kind.
- **access variant** — the configuration and authority egma uses for that connection kind, such as a Retell API key, a public E.164 number, a LiveKit project key pair, or a customer token endpoint. Two access variants can use the same connection kind.
- **modality** — `voice` or `chat`. Decides which layer is under test: chat exercises the harness (prompt, reasoning, tools); voice exercises the harness *plus* the speech stack.
- **product label** — the human name shown for one supported combination of platform, connection kind, access variant, and modality. It explains the choice; it is not another technical identity.
- **environment** — a label.

Current supported combinations are:

| Agent platform | Connection kind | Access variant | Modality | Product label |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Retell | `retell_chat_api` | Retell API key | chat | Retell chat |
| Retell | `phone_number` | Public E.164 number | voice | Retell phone |
| LiveKit Agents | `livekit_room` | Project key pair | voice | LiveKit project credentials |
| LiveKit Agents | `livekit_room` | Customer token endpoint | voice | LiveKit token endpoint |
| Any or unknown | `phone_number` | Public E.164 number | voice | Phone number |

**production ingestion** — how egma receives evidence of real production conversations. It is separate from a simulation connection. An agent platform may have platform-specific ingestion strategies, such as polling Retell's calls API or receiving LiveKit spans through OTLP. Production-ingestion ownership and configuration are settled by their own design, not inferred from a connection kind or access variant. Added 2026-08-19 during the production-monitoring grilling.

**monitoring setup** — the customer configuration that lets egma receive production evidence from one agent platform. Setup starts by selecting the agent platform and then follows that platform's required steps; one setup may select several agents reported by that platform. The platform-specific production-ingestion process runs from this setup. A monitoring setup is not a simulation connection. Added 2026-08-19 during the production-monitoring grilling.

**A simulation records the connection it ran over, and this is load-bearing.** 8 kHz μ-law and WebRTC produce *different units*: the codec destroys information audio graders need and inflates every latency number. Comparing scores across connection types is invalid. See [How to connect to a voice agent, per framework](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/04-voice-agent-connection-per-framework.md).

## The caller

**persona** — the synthetic person who calls the agent. Who they are: manner, patience, accent, background noise, and how they behave under friction. A first-class, reusable, versioned entity. A persona is either **Egma-provided** and shared read-only, or **Custom** and owned by one project.

**persona version** — one immutable, executable form of a persona. It owns the caller's traits and the complete model selection used to bring that caller to life: LLM provider and model, STT provider and model, and TTS provider, model, voice ID, and speed. The technical voice has no second home in traits or platform settings. Editing any of these facts creates a new persona version.

A persona says nothing about *what* the caller wants — that's the test's scenario. The same persona calls about many different things.

Every project carries one active **default persona** — a project choice, not a persona type. A new project points at Egma's shared default persona. A project may point at any active Egma-provided or Custom persona available to it instead. A default cannot be archived until the project pointer moves. A test created naming no callers receives this pointer, so authoring a first test never waits on authoring a caller.

In a transcript the two speakers are labelled **`human:`** and **`agent:`**.

> Renamed from `digital human` on 2026-08-05 (public issue #8). `digital human` was originally chosen over `persona` for saying plainly that the caller is synthetic — accepting that users arriving from other tools would say "persona" and need correcting. They did say it, and the correcting bought nothing: `persona` is the voice industry's near-unanimous term, and now it is egma's. Also considered and still not chosen: `simulant`, `virtual human`, `synthetic user`, `phantom`, `surrogate`.

## The specification

**test** — one authored specification. Anthropic's *task*. Owned by the project and contained by exactly one test suite. It never belongs or applies to named agents. It holds:

- **the scenario** — the situation, as the test's own content. What the caller wants and the circumstances. Not a separate entity.
- **personas** — an array. One to start; several when a scenario should be checked against several kinds of caller. Three personas on a test means running it produces three simulations.
- **expected behaviors** — an ordered list of **plain sentences** about what should happen, **at least one, enforced at write time**. A test with no expected behaviors is unfalsifiable and is rejected, not silently accepted. The sentences carry no metadata: per-behavior priorities were retired 2026-08-14 (grader-redesign grilling) — under binary scoring every behavior must hold, so a priority had nothing left to say. Replaced *the expected outcome* (one paragraph of end state) on 2026-08-05 in the test-factory grilling: a list buys per-behavior verdicts, and Coval deprecated its output-shaped field for exactly this shape. Entries may describe conduct along the way or the state afterwards; true outcome *verification* against customer systems returns with verification hooks.
- **graders** — none named on the test. The project's seeded expected-behaviors copy and every other running grader apply to every test on their own; per-test attachment (the grader array and `test_grader` junction) was dropped 2026-08-14 and returns, if needed, as grader-side filters in the custom-grader era. Every test can still fail from birth — the seeded copy sees to it. History: ADR-0004 superseded *at least one grader at write time*; [ADR-0009](docs/adr/0009-grader-library-and-running-copies.md) superseded the array.

**Tests are modality-agnostic.** A test never mentions voice or chat. This buys the best diagnostic in the product: run the same test over chat and over voice, and the difference isolates the failure. Passes on text, fails on voice → the prompt is fine and the speech stack is broken. Fails on both → it's the reasoning.

**test suite** — an unversioned, named container for tests normally run and reviewed together. A user creates it before the first test; the one clean-cutover exception is the ordinary `Default` suite created around existing tests by the one-time migration. Suites are flat, unordered, and may be empty. Every test belongs to exactly one suite for its lifetime; tests never move between suites. A suite's name may change. Deleting a suite deletes every test it contains, after a warning, and neither the suite nor those tests can be restored; post-cutover runs that already used them remain historical facts and show the suite's last name marked as deleted. One test may also be deleted permanently without deleting its suite. A suite never carries graders, agents, connections, or execution settings. See [ADR-0013](docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md).

## Mock tools

**mock tool** — a project-owned stand-in for one of the agent's tools: the tool's name, and the answer egma serves when the agent calls it during a simulation. The answer may be an error — that is how a test forces the failure branch — and may carry a delay, so a mocked backend takes as long as the real one would. **Matching is by tool name, strictly: one answer per tool.** A mock tool never reads a call's arguments; wrong arguments are caught by grading, not matching, because the arguments are on the record either way. Chosen over `tool mock` because it is the word users arrive with (Cekura, Vapi) — the persona lesson, applied the cheap way this time. Added 2026-08-09, mock-tools grilling.

**Project mock tools apply to every test by default; a test overrides per scenario, and the override is the branching mechanism.** "The calendar has no free slots" is the same test with one mock tool overridden. A mock tool may name the agents it applies to (default: all) — agent *affinity* without agent *ownership*, so prompt variants are always tested against one world and their comparison stays honest. Mock tools are deliberately **unversioned** — the one authored thing that is (decided 2026-08-09, same grilling): an edit overwrites, and history lives elsewhere — every answer a simulation was served is on that simulation's record, and a run snapshots its resolved answers at creation, so one run always sees one world. The never-overwritten rule stands everywhere else; versioning returns if cross-run change detection ever demands it.

**Unmocked tools run real, and unobserved.** A tool no mock tool covers runs its real implementation natively — egma is not in that path and does not see the call. Decided 2026-08-09, reversing the same session's earlier design (every call observed and stamped `pass-through`): the receipt required wrapping every tool, and wrapping only what egma answers won. The record's honesty is at the **tool grain**, from discovery: which of the agent's tools were covered by mock tools and which were not. That is the **coverage stamp** (`mock_tool_coverage` on a simulation), and its absence is a fact of its own — no stamp means nothing ever asked the agent what tools it has, while three empty lists mean the asking happened and nothing came back. A mocked simulation and an unmocked one remain **different units**, exactly as two audio bands are, and the record is what enforces it.

**egma SDK** — the piece of egma a customer installs inside their own agent's process. Its first job is the mock-tools seam for LiveKit agents: report the agent's tool list when the session starts, then wrap exactly the tools this simulation mocks — each wrapped call goes to egma's participant over in-room RPC and egma answers with the mock. Tools egma does not answer stay native. In a room with no egma participant it is inert, so production behavior is untouched by construction. One public verb, awaited once where the session is built: `await mockable(agent, ctx, session)` — the wait is structural, because the tool list has to have been reported before the agent's first tool call. See [ADR-0008](docs/adr/0008-mock-tools-are-served-over-in-room-rpc.md). Added 2026-08-09, mock-tools grilling.

## Execution

**run** — one execution of one complete test suite against one agent over one connection. Every test in the suite runs; no agent relationship filters the suite. ISTQB's *test run*: *"the execution of a test suite on a specific version of the test object."* The object a results page shows and CI gates on. The UI labels the surface **Simulations → Runs** in navigation — the group supplies the first word — and **simulation runs** in page headings; the word everywhere else stays `run` (settled 2026-08-16, monitoring grilling; regrouped 2026-08-19, product-UI ticket 17). A run may have a user-written name, but does not require one. …1280 tokens truncated…ans, the pages' analytics and errors, the box's vitals. Never a customer's data and never in ClickHouse — `trace` and `span` stay conversation words, and egma's own telemetry never shares the trace store's pipe. Behind one flag, `EGMA_TELEMETRY`, off by default everywhere; hosted egma turns it on and points it at PostHog and CloudWatch. Added 2026-08-17, observability effort; see [ADR-0010](docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md).

## Judging

**grader** — a running copy of a grader-library entry: the row that judges, and the thing verdict rows name. Created by pressing **Use** on a library entry, or seeded at project creation. It points at its entry (`library_id` — the connecting tissue, never null, never orphaned: deleting a referenced entry is refused), carries the entry's `type`, and holds its **filled-in values** — latency's `[{metric, bound}]` — in immutable versions; editing the values mints the next version, and a run pins the versions it executed. Each grader version also points at one immutable grader-library definition version. The prompt or code is shared once at the library layer, never copied into each project, while the exact definition used by an old run stays reconstructable. Redefined 2026-08-19, model-execution cutover; the word previously named the authored logic itself.

**The distinction that matters: a metric measures, a grader judges.** Nobody wrote down that the call took four minutes — it just happened. Someone had to decide that verifying identity before disclosing a balance matters, and write the criteria. That's the line.

They connect in one direction: **a grader may read a metric.** *"Fail if p90 response time exceeds 2 seconds"* is a grader whose input is a measurement. So latency is always known, and only becomes a verdict if you ask for one.

A grader declares:

- **required** — `true` (default): the test cannot pass unless this copy fully passes. `false`: a **diagnostic** — judged, displayed with its fraction, never able to fail anything. τ2-bench's outside-the-reward-basis components, and the only loudness switch v0 has. Replaces the P0/P1/P2 priority ladder, retired 2026-08-14, grader-redesign grilling.
- **its scope** — the whole answer to where the copy applies: two switches — **judges simulations** (default on) and **judges production** (default off, with the production sampling rate) — and a **filter** under each switch. `both` retired 2026-08-20, grader-scope grilling: it was two switches written as one word, and the one word hid the two opposite safe defaults (simulations exist to be judged; production judging spends money on traffic nobody asked egma to create). Dormant is **no copy at all** — the switches say where an existing copy applies, not whether it exists; pressing Use is still the enabling and deleting the copy is the off-switch.
- **which modalities it can score** (declared by its library entry). *"Didn't interrupt the caller"* is meaningless on chat. A grader that can't score the modality is **skipped**, and the results view must say *skipped*, not *failed*.

**grader library** — the shelf of grader definitions: `grader_library` holds each stable library identity and immutable definition versions hold its executable prompt, output definition, parameter schema, or code. An entry declares its **type** — `llm_as_judge` or `code`; reserved: `human`, `ml_model`, `external`. **Owner derives from tenancy**: null organization and project means egma owns the entry — the one deliberate exception to hard-required tenancy — seeded from a catalog in egma's code. When an Egma release changes a definition, reconciliation mints one new shared definition version and new grader versions for active running copies. New runs pin those versions; old runs keep the old definition through their already-pinned grader versions. No definition is copied per project, and no catalog edit changes the meaning of an old verdict. Team-authored entries land in the same library with tenancy set, when custom authoring arrives. Redefined 2026-08-19, model-execution cutover.

**predefined grader** — a library entry egma owns and ships. v0 ships two: **expected_behaviors** (`llm_as_judge`) and **latency** (`code`). Replaces *built-in grader*, 2026-08-14 — `predefined` is the word users arrive with (Cekura), the persona lesson applied the cheap way again.

**rubric** — the criteria text an `llm_as_judge` grader carries. Anthropic's word. Added 2026-08-07; repointed from the retired `llm_rubric` type, 2026-08-14.

**assertion** — one 0-or-1 check inside a grader. A grader holds one or more assertions, and each is judged in isolation: for an LLM-judged grader, one independent judge call per assertion — Anthropic's per-dimension isolation, which is how the engine has run since the grading effort. The expected-behaviors grader's assertions are the test's own expected behaviors; a code grader's assertions are the entries in its configuration. Un-banned and adopted 2026-08-14, grader-redesign grilling: the word once banned as a synonym for a whole grader now names the level below it, and the old ban stands exactly there — an assertion is never a grader. One word at every layer: the verdict store's column is `assertion` too (renamed from `dimension` by the same grilling — the store is pre-launch and small, so the rename is cheap).

**Applicability: a running copy applies to everything its switches and filters allow.** There is still no per-test attachment — the `test_grader` junction stays dropped, and a test names no graders; narrowing is declared grader-side, so a check written once judges everything it covers without anyone remembering to attach it. A copy whose switch or filter excludes a conversation writes no verdict rows at all — absent, never `skipped`, which keeps meaning "applied but could not score the modality". Settled 2026-08-20, grader-scope grilling: the filters deferred by the grader-redesign spec arrived, per side — see the grader-scope spec. **Never attached to a suite** stands untouched.

**filter** — the where/and rows under one switch of a running copy's scope: `{fact, any_of | none_of, values}`, rows joined by AND, at most one row per fact, values inside a row OR'd; empty means everything that switch allows. Facts come from a **fact catalog** in egma's code that declares each fact's value source, its operators, and which sides can answer it — `agent` on both sides, `test` on simulations only in v1 — so the production builder never offers a fact a live call cannot answer, and an unanswerable rule is unrepresentable rather than refused. A filter is live and unversioned, like the switches: what a grader judges by is versioned; where it applies is not. Added 2026-08-20, grader-scope grilling.

**scope_editable** — on the library entry: whether copies of it may re-aim their scope. Using an egma-defined grader means using it **as is** — you edit what egma allows; false locks the whole scope (switches, rate, both filters) on every copy, seeded or Use-created. expected_behaviors ships locked (judges simulations on, production off, no filter), which also enforces that it can never judge a live call — a production trace has no test to judge against; latency ships editable. `required` is not scope — how loudly, not where — and stays editable on locked copies. Forking a grader is not a v1 concept. Added 2026-08-20, grader-scope grilling.

**expected-behaviors grader** — the predefined `llm_as_judge` entry that judges a simulation against its test's expected behaviors. Its assertions are the test's own sentences — supplied per test at judging time, one isolated judge call each ([ADR-0007](docs/adr/0007-grading-runs-in-its-own-service.md)) — so the entry itself defines no assertions and **Use** asks nothing. In the library like any entry, and **auto-seeded as an active running copy in every new project** (judges simulations only, required, locked as-is by its entry's `scope_editable: false`), so a first run is judged with zero setup. Structurally simulations-only: a production trace has no test, and the locked scope is what enforces it. Supersedes ADR-0004's never-a-row clause — see [ADR-0009](docs/adr/0009-grader-library-and-running-copies.md); falsifiability still lives on the behaviors list, required non-empty at write time, exactly as ADR-0004 placed it.

**verdict** — `passed`, `failed`, `skipped`, or `errored`, written **one row per assertion**. `skipped` and `errored` are load-bearing and must never be collapsed into `failed`: a test that couldn't run is not a test that failed, and a check that couldn't read its inputs didn't fail either. A verdict row carries a 0–1 score, a one-line rationale (on an `errored` row, the plain-prose reason judging broke), the turns it cites, and its assertion's **key** — the behavior's position in the pinned test version, the config entry's index — never the content, which is read from the pinned versions at display time. **Scoring is binary**: a grader's fraction (passed ÷ counted, skipped out of the denominator) is reported for diagnosis and decides nothing; a test passes in a run when every applicable `required` copy fully passes across all its simulations. Overall outcomes are always computed from verdict rows at read time, never stored. Thresholds, weights, and human corrections are designed and deferred — see the grader-redesign spec. Extended 2026-08-07; rewritten 2026-08-14, grader-redesign grilling.

## The onboarding surface

**wizard** — the complete terminal experience `npx egma` presents when run bare: its UI, the intelligent work performed by the developer's local coding agent, and the deterministic work performed through the same CLI modules as the headless verbs. It takes a developer from nothing to a running first run. The internal split is not a second customer experience, and the wizard is never a second code path. Clarified 2026-08-09 during the self-hosted phone onboarding grilling; originally added 2026-08-06 ([ADR-0006](docs/adr/0006-onboarding-wizard-drives-the-customers-coding-agent.md)).

**egma folder** — the `egma/` directory in the customer's repo: project, agent, and connection config; one directory per test suite under `tests/`; a `suite.yaml` carrying that suite's stable ID and mutable name; one markdown file per test inside its suite directory; and one file for the project's mock tools. One repository may contain several suites. A suite directory is only a local path: moving or renaming it changes no product identity or name. Editing `suite.yaml` changes the suite name on push. The folder is committed, never gitignored; nothing secret ever lands in it. The platform remains the store of record — the folder is a working copy.

**platform binding** — the non-secret platform URL written in `egma/config.yaml` beside the resource identifiers that platform owns. It chooses the platform that receives those identifiers; credentials and a platform-instance identity are never part of the binding. An unbound repository uses hosted egma at `app.egma.ai`. See [ADR-0012](docs/adr/0012-agent-repositories-bind-to-a-platform-url.md).

**pull / push** — the explicit sync verbs between the egma folder and the platform, on git's model: `pull` writes the platform's current versions into files; `push` uploads and **refuses** when the platform has moved since the last pull. **That refusal is a property of versioned things**: a test earns it, and so do the mock-tool overrides that version with it. A project mock tool is unversioned by decision, so it has no version to have moved — pushing `egma/mock-tools.md` is last-write-wins, and a teammate's edit in between is not detected; the run's snapshot and the answers on the record carry that history instead. Sync is always a verb a developer runs, never a background process — two silently-syncing authoring surfaces are the documented failure (Humanloop's copy-drift).

## Banned words

Do not use these — in code, schema, API, docs or UI.

| Don't use | Why | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `eval`, `evaluation` | Everyone says it, nobody agrees what it points at | nothing — informal prose only |
| `evaluator` | Half the industry means the test, the other half the thing scoring it | `grader` |
| `scorer`, `check` | Borrowed words for the judging job — one word per level | `grader` for the authored logic, `assertion` for one criterion inside it |
| `dimension` | The verdict store's old column name for it — one entity, one word, at every layer including storage | `assertion` |
| `gate` | Considered for the must-pass flag during the grader redesign, not chosen | `required` |
| `built-in grader` | Renamed 2026-08-14 — `predefined` is the word users arrive with (Cekura) | `predefined grader` |
| `metric` *for scoring logic* | A metric measures, a grader judges | `grader` |
| `digital human` | The old name, renamed 2026-08-05 — one entity, one word | `persona` |
| `simulant`, `virtual human`, `synthetic user`, `digital twin` | Considered, not chosen | `persona` |
| `scenario` *as an entity* | It's what a test says, not a thing of its own | a field on `test` |
| `session` *for a conversation* | Same thing as a simulation | `simulation` |
| `trial`, `attempt`, `iteration` | Running a test twice just makes two simulations | `simulation` |
| `call` | Half of them are chats | `simulation` |
| `conversation` | Same thing as a simulation | `simulation` |
| `caller` | Breaks the moment it's a chat | `persona` |
| `result` *as an entity* | A result is "passed" or "failed" — it isn't the recording | `verdict`, or the simulation itself |
| `experiment`, `batch` | Borrowed from a different world | `run` |
| `expected outcome` *as a test field* | Replaced 2026-08-05 — the test's expectations are a list of behaviors, not one paragraph of end state | `expected behaviors` |
| `tool mock` | The inverted form of the entity's name — one entity, one word | `mock tool` |
| `stub`, `fake` *for a mock tool* | Same job, one word | `mock tool` |

**One carve-out, and it is not a loophole.** `session` **is the right word for a signed-in browser session**, and the ban does not reach it. The auth provider owns a `session` table, the provider seam's fourth method is `revokeSession`, and [ADR-0001](docs/adr/0001-auth-provider-owns-identity-only.md) and the control-plane spec both require the word in that sense — so the unqualified ban forbade what the decision records mandate, which is how a glossary stops being consulted. Added 2026-08-01 after the control-plane code review found the contradiction, with roughly ninety correct uses already in the codebase. The ban stands exactly where it was aimed: **`session` never names a conversation.** A simulation is a simulation.

The same carve-out covers one more seam, for the same reason: **the Agent Client Protocol names its connection to a driven coding agent a `session`** (`session/new`, `session/prompt`, `session/request_permission` are the wire methods), and [ADR-0006](docs/adr/0006-onboarding-wizard-drives-the-customers-coding-agent.md) mandates that SDK — so the CLI's ACP seam uses the protocol's word as-is, exactly as the auth seam uses the provider's. Added 2026-08-06 after the walking-skeleton code review hit the contradiction. Both carve-outs point the same direction: a `session` is standing machinery you connect to, never the conversation a persona has with an agent.

## Reserved words

Good words. Each means exactly one thing and is never borrowed for another.

| Word | Always means | Never means |
|---|---|---|
| `user` | the developer using egma | the persona |
| `customer` | the organization paying for egma | the persona |
| `agent` | the voice agent under test | egma's side of the call |
| `human` | the caller's side of a transcript | a real person reviewing results |
| `project` | the tenancy container below the organization | any resource inside one — LangSmith's collision, where "project" is a resource four levels beneath a "workspace" container |
| `trace` | one conversation end to end, simulated or real — a storage-layer word that never appears in a UI | a UI-facing name for a simulation |
| `span` | one timed thing inside a trace — a storage-layer word that never appears in a UI | a turn specifically; a turn is one kind of span |

`trace` and `span` were put on this list by [The unified ClickHouse trace schema](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/09-unified-clickhouse-trace-schema.md), which needed a word for a conversation that might not be a simulation: a production trace has no test, no run and no persona, so `simulation` cannot name it. A simulation *is* a trace — one carrying a `run_id`. Recorded here 2026-08-02 after a trace-store code review found the ticket's instruction had never landed in this file.

`global` was briefly the label over the standing pair (Agents, Graders), added 2026-08-19 by [17 — Group the navigation](.scratch/product-ui/issues/17-group-navigation-under-global-simulations-and-monitoring.md) with its objection recorded: nothing under it was global, and a reader could predict organization-wide settings behind the word. The recorded reopen condition — first-user evidence of the misread — arrived 2026-08-20 as the developer's own first look, and the label was dropped the same day: the pair now sits as an unlabeled cluster above Simulations and Monitoring. The word is free again and means nothing in this product.

## Mapping to Anthropic's taxonomy

| Anthropic | egma | Note |
|---|---|---|
| evaluation suite | **test suite** | egma's is a named container, not a saved selector or execution plan |
| task | **test** | |
| trial | **simulation** | |
| *(unnamed)* | **run** | Anthropic leaves this slot empty; 8 of 10 voice vendors call it a run |
| transcript / trajectory | **transcript** | |
| outcome | **outcome** | |
| grader | **grader** | |
| assertion (sometimes called checks) | **assertion** | Same word; one 0-or-1 check inside a grader |
| tracked metrics | **metric** | A field, not an entity |
| agent harness | **agent** + **connection** | Split, because reaching the agent is a first-class problem in voice |
| *(none)* | **persona** | Anthropic's taxonomy has one agent; a voice conversation has two participants |

## Deferred

Named here so the boundary is clear; decided elsewhere.

- **What a grader is made of** was settled 2026-08-07 by the grading effort (`.scratch/grading/spec.md`) and **re-settled 2026-08-14 by the grader redesign** (`.scratch/grader-redesign/spec.md`): a library of definitions, running copies, assertions, binary scoring. Where the two disagree, the redesign wins.
- **Thresholds, weights, filters, custom authoring, human corrections, the `ml_model` and `external` types, and any warn tier** — each designed with a named home and deferred, in the grader-redesign spec's future-work section. Deliberately not sketched anywhere else, so the sketch cannot fork.
- **Classification** — labels that segment without judging: sentiment, topic of a conversation, where it dropped off. A third concept beside measure (a number, automatic) and grader (a verdict, chosen): a label, chosen. Every surveyed vendor ships it; none names it. Deliberately deferred so labels are never wedged into verdicts.
- **Whether a persona behaves like a real caller**, and how egma would claim it does, is not yet specified. It is the credibility floor of the product.
- **Where personas come from.** Research strongly favours grounding them in the customer's own recordings over describing them from demographics.
- **Chain-consistent mock worlds** — bundles that keep `lookup_user` → account → booking data coherent across mock tools (the "John Smith world"). Deliberately deferred: project defaults plus per-test overrides carry v1, and a bundle entity can grow out of them if incoherence actually bites. Named 2026-08-09, mock-tools grilling.
